items.title: Knicks Bulletin: ‘I was raised by Wolves’
items.author: Antonio Losada
items.content:
I thought yesterday’s game was over by the end of the third quarter…

…only for these fools to nearly drop it. Good thing, they did not.

Here’s a bunch of quotes coming off Minnesota as the boys return home once and for all.

On finishing the road trip with a victory over Minnesota:

“Great to finish off a road trip, getting a win in a pretty tough environment by a well-coached team. It’ll make the plane ride a little bit better going home.”

On the Knicks’ fourth-quarter offensive collapse against the Timberwolves:

“Our execution the first three quarters was at a pretty high level against this team. And then you give them credit. Fourth quarter, they did a phenomenal job defensively, kind of bogged us down. The ball and the pace offensively in the frontcourt wasn’t popping like it was the first three quarters.”

On the Knicks winning the battle for loose balls despite struggling offensively in the fourth quarter:

“The thing that saved us was winning the 50-50 ballgame. We were 13-for-14 in that area, and that was huge for us because we had trouble scoring in the fourth.”

On beating his former team as an NBA champion with the Knicks:

“I was raised by Wolves, but it was Knicks in 5 at the end.”

On why the Knicks don’t need to win games convincingly:

“For ‘Dancing with the Stars.’ For us, at the end of the day, as long as we win, this team is just trying to stack the number on the left side.”

On the importance of winning games in different ways:

“If you wanna win a championship, you gotta be ready to win in any way possible, because you never know what the game will be.”

On his uncertain contract situation and remaining focused on his responsibilities to the Knicks:

“I got a job to do, at the end of the day. I gotta come here and put that jersey on and do what’s best for my brothers and the guys they have in my locker room. So, I’m just here to do my job.”

On refusing to let his contract situation distract him from performing:

“I gotta put that jersey on and put the best performance out there for my teammates. So, that’s all I really think about.”

On his emotional attachment to Minnesota:

“I still have so much love for this place. It doesn’t go away. I think it’s actually grown as I’ve been away. I think that, even for me and my dad, we were just driving around the city and just going to places. We went to eat at a spot we love to go here. It always hits home. This is the last place that I got to play basketball with my mom. I got to see the kids be young before now. Jolani, my niece, who was in my rookie of the year photo actually in here, she was a baby, and now she’s in high school. It’s a different part of life, but it’s a part of life that I really enjoy.”

On returning to Minnesota as an NBA champion:

“It’s always great to be home and to be back here. Nine years of my life, some amazing years, amazing moments. Yeah, it’s special to be back. Obviously, it’s bittersweet to come back with a championship because I wanted to win it here so bad for the city, for Minneapolis, for Minnesota, for all the people who haven’t seen an NBA championship here. But it’s great to be able to come back and to be able to see friends, people I call family here.”

On the release of the new Grand Theft Auto game and his excitement to play it:

“I haven’t played the game yet, but I’ve heard it’s a hell of a game. So shout-out to Rockstar [Games] and 2K and Take-Two [Interactive]; they did a good job with that one. It’s fun, man. The world is taken over by ‘GTA,’ as it rightfully should be.”

On his Grand Theft Alvarado nickname and his history with the video game:

“I was a big fan of it before my name. It was just a cool name that I had, so it makes it even better when I play the new one. Got the name for it; now, play the game.”

On how much his life has changed since GTA V dropped:

“Thirteen years ago, I wouldn’t even be talking to you, I promise you that. It’s a long journey, fun journey, one hell of a ride. Still with it.”

On the Knicks nearly blowing their lead against Minnesota:

“It was hectic. We gotta get better at finishing a game like that. But it’s a win, 3-1 on the road trip. We’ll take it.”

On the criticism Karl-Anthony Towns faced during his Timberwolves years:

“Particularly when he started his playoff journey, how much flak he had gotten.”

On Towns leading the Wolves to the Western Conference Finals:

“We don’t do it without him in all facets of the game, whether it be his defense in the Phoenix series, the only guy who held us in the game in Game 7 in Denver when we had nothing else going until we could find it in the second half. Those are the little moments that spring to mind. There are many others along the way. And he kind of grew into that and then was able to build on that with an experienced team where he fit into in New York.”

On watching Towns succeed in the Knicks’ championship run:

“It was fun to see him at the heart of it, too. Especially as they were kind of tweaking their offense going along and all of his skills came to the surface through that.”

On the similarities between Towns and LaMelo Ball:

“They play with a lot of expression to their game and people interpret that or they don’t like that. But it doesn’t mean that A) they’re not super talented players, of course, and B) they can’t play winning basketball. Sometimes it’s as much of the environment that people might be judging them unfairly through, if that makes sense.

“They both are really selfless in the way that they play. But maybe some of their expressions and the way that they carry themselves on the court draws a lot of attention and they get judged unfairly for that, too. They’re actually incredibly selfless. They both play with a lot of joy.

“They’re incredible people. Just great teammates, fun to be around, always bring the same energy every day. Very coachable.”

Yankees 2026 Roster Report Cards: George Lombard Jr.
items.author: Jonathan Farrar
items.content:
Few positions, or the players manning them, have been debated as intensely as shortstop for the New York Yankees over the last several seasons. Heading into 2026, many fans hoped the club would find a way to move on from the Anthony Volpe experience. However, the club made no external moves and started the season with José Caballero slotted in at the position as the team waited for a rehabbing Volpe to return.

Along the way, injuries and performance, both struggles by the incumbents and red-hot play in the minors, led the Yankees to hand the reins at shortstop over to 21-year-old George Lombard Jr. The rookie would spend August, September, and October at shortstop for the Yankees in what really is the throne of NYC. 

In terms of how it went, the staff here at PSA averaged out to a B-minus. In academic speak, that would mean Lombard understood the core material and performed above average, but did not master the assignment.

42 G, 166 PA, 23 R, 36 H, 4 2B, 1 3B, 7 HR, 22 RBI, 2 SB, .237/.285/.414, 92 OPS+, 93 wRC+, 0.4 fWAR, 1.1 bWAR.

Pre-arbitration eligible.

Before reaching the show, Lombard was on an absolute tear in the minors. Starting the season in Double-A, he hit .312 with a .971 OPS in 20 games, which earned him a ticket to Scranton. Lombard’s season looked like it might be coming off the rails after an adjustment period, and then he sprained two fingers, which sidelined him for a month and caused him to miss the MLB Futures Game. However, he came back in mid-July and forced the Yankees’ hand right before the Trade Deadline, going on a 14-game heater to the tune of a .377 average, .477 OBP, and 1.081 OPS.

On August 4th, after surviving the Trade Deadline himself, and with the Yankees not acquiring an outside option at shortstop, the club called Lombard up to the show. The kid finished the minor league season slashing .284/.411/.498 with 12 home runs. This performance led Baseball America to name him the Yankees’ Minor League Player of the Year for 2026.

Lombard’s 2026 season at the professional level, and the basis for our grading, really is a story of three parts. The first was a euphoric honeymoon stage. Lombard committed just one error in his first 14 games and racked up eight Defensive Runs Saved (DRS) in his first 100 innings, looking like a potential Platinum Glove winner. This all came as he homered in his first pro at-bat and slashed .320/.393/.560 with a .953 OPS across his first 25 at-bats. It was too good to be true.

After the rise came the fall, as Lombard slumped with the glove and bat. In late August, Lombard made the wrong kind of history, committing an error in six straight games and tying a 105-year-old franchise record. With the stick, big league pitchers started getting him to chase and roll over breaking balls, causing his average to sink to .217 by mid-September. The vibes from some fans really went from “next” to “next Volpe.”

To the kid’s credit, he righted the ship down the stretch and saved himself in the third act. From September 9th through the end of the regular season, Lombard’s defense stabilized to league average, and he hit five home runs in his final 16 games. He carried that confidence into the postseason, going 3-for-4 in the Wild Card opener against Boston and finishing October batting .333 (6-for-18), albeit with an error in the ALDS.

I’ll save the hype train for future preview articles. However, despite only having an 86 mph average exit velocity, Lombard finished the season pacing for 27 home runs over 162 games. There’s also a lot of room for growth, as Lombard had a 17.3 percent walk rate at Triple-A and only a six percent rate in the majors through his first 42 games, or essentially a quarter of a season. The defense, especially when playing beside a big league-quality third baseman, was fine for someone who was just a few months into being able to buy an adult beverage.

Lombard’s minor league season was an A+, while his rookie season comes in at a B-. With some growing pains behind us and a few more likely ahead, here’s to hoping Lombard can continue to improve and develop into a difference-maker. What grade would you circle in red for Lombard’s 2026 season, and what do you predict he’s produce next season?

See more of the Yankees Roster Report Card series here.

items.title: Vinales withdraws after single MotoGP session in Portugal
items.author: Valentin Khorounzhiy
items.content:
Maverick Vinales has pulled out of the second-to-last round of the 2026 MotoGP season, replaced by KTM test rider Pol Espargaro.

Vinales, who does not have a ride for 2027 and remains limited by the shoulder injury he sustained last year, is now also in doubt for the season finale in Valencia, which was set to mark his final appearance as a full-time MotoGP rider for the time being.

The 31-year-old has spent the entire campaign struggling to be competitive due to the after-effects of that 2025 shoulder injury at the Sachsenring. A follow-up operation and various courses of treatment have allowed him to recover his fitness for daily life, but when it came to riding in MotoGP he has encountered persistent issues with pain and inflammation.

The lack of any recent competitive track record meant KTM abandoned the plan to promote him to the factory outfit from satellite team Tech3, and he was then left out of Tech3's 2027 line-up, too.

Ahead of Portimao, Vinales said that the weekend off between Qatar and Portugal allowed him to improve his condition - but was wary of how his body would react to riding the KTM RC16 again.

"If I'm riding right now, I mentioned many times, one [reason] is for my salary, and the second is because my team is here, and I want to race for them, and I don't want someone [else] riding my bike."

But on Friday, after placing 19th in the opening practice session, with 17 laps completed, Vinales has called time on his Portimao outing.

"It was a really difficult decision, because I want to keep pushing, but we have decided it is best to stop," he lamented. "The important thing is to avoid any more damage to my shoulder and any dangerous situations on track, and I will continue to focus on my recovery.

"It's disappointing, especially after all the work I've put in to get back here, but I have to listen to my body."

Tech3 says Vinales "will continue to assess his condition" ahead of the Valencia finale.

items.title: Yankees sign Jonathan Loáisiga to two-year deal
items.author: John Griffin
items.content:
So far this winter, the bullpen has been a clear priority for the Yankees, who saw no fewer than four important relievers from the 2026 season become free agents. After re-signing Tim Hill and bringing back David Bednar on the qualifying offer, the team has now made its third addition to the bullpen, coming to terms with old friend Jonathan Loáisiga on a two-year deal with a team option for 2029.

Canal 4 News in Loáisiga’s native Nicaragua had the news late last night, the man himself hinted at it with a picture of the NYC skyline on his Instagram story, and Jorge Castillo of ESPN confirmed it this morning. MLB.com’s Mark Feinsand reported the total outlay of the contract as $18 million across the two years and buyout.

Yankees fans are, of course, very familiar with the man nicknamed Johnny Lasagna. Signed as a minor-league free agent in 2016 after a couple years in the Giants’ organization, Loáisiga spent parts of eight seasons with the big league club, and served as the bullpen’s ace fireman/setup man in 2021 and the second half of 2022. Injuries and ineffectiveness plagued the right-hander for the next three seasons, however, and after a lackluster 2025, the Bombers declined his team option for 2026.

It turned out to be the best thing for him. After sitting on the market for most of the winter, Loáisiga signed a minor-league free agent deal with the Diamondbacks last January. He made the team out of spring training, stayed healthy for a full season for the first time in five years, and put together one of the best seasons of his career, posting a 2.42 ERA in 67 innings. Perhaps more importantly, his advanced metrics were some of the best of his career, and helps explain why there were so many suitors for the recently-turned 32-year-old (the Mets, Phillies, Dodgers, and Blue Jays were all reportedly in on him).

Despite the small time apart, though, Loáisiga is not exactly the same pitcher who Yankee fans remember. Gone are the days where he threw the sinker like Mariano Rivera threw the cutter, i.e., pretty much every pitch. Although it’s still his main offering (he threw it 35 percent of the time last year), that is a far cry from the 54-to-69-percent usage rates from his first Yankees stint; in its stead, he’s upped his changeup, fastball, and cutter.

While nobody would ever consider Loáisiga a strikeout pitcher, these changes oversaw a slight bump in strikeout percentage to 18.4 percent from his 16.6-percent rate between 2022-24 and a slight drop in walk rate to a career-best 5.0 percent, all without sacrificing ground-ball rate. The question will just be how his body holds up after an actual full, healthy season.

Even with Loáisiga, Hill, and Bednar back in the fold, the Yankees are probably not yet done looking at bullpen arms — assuming they ever truly feel like they have enough bullpen arms. At this point, though, the Yankees have successfully turned it from a “need” to a “want,” as they’re no longer so thin out there that Yerry De los Santos and Angel Chivilli were listed as two of the team’s higher-leverage relief arms on the FanGraphs Depth Chart.

One could, of course, absolutely still argue that they still need a big swing-and-miss arm in the ’pen, as they’re still lacking in that regard and not everyone should be a pitch-to-contact guy. As we wait for the league to come to a screeching halt in 10 days due to the owners’ insistence on a lockout, getting some things crossed off the winter to-do list is certainly not a bad thing, and Loáisiga checks another box.

items.title: From plumbing to Picnic PostNL – The Dutch team's newest recruit with dreams of Amstel Gold Race and riding with Wout van Aert
items.author: cyclingnews@futurenet.com (Dani Ostanek)
items.content:
The lowest-ranked team in the WorldTour last year, Picnic PostNL, have made plenty of changes to their roster next season, with nine new faces and counting.

Joining the Dutch team in their quest for more success in 2027 is Belgian racer Daan Depuydt, who comes on board from Continental squad Baloise Verzekeringen-Het Poetsbureau Lions.

The 23-year-old, who previously raced at amateur level, enjoyed several standout rides this year, including a Tour de Limousin stage win and three top-10 finishes at the Tour de Wallonie. His rise to the WorldTour has been a rapid one, given he was working as a plumber just a few years ago.

Depuydt, who also did odd jobs as a gardener and electrician, told that, "Actually, I was never really consciously focused on landing a professional contract. I just raced because I enjoyed it."

He primarily raced on the mountain bike as a junior, picking up four Belgian titles before struggling with back injuries. On the road, he raced in Belgium with amateur squad VP Consulting before catching the eye of Baloise-Het Poetsbureau – Sven Nys' team – with a stage win at the Triptyque Ardennais in 2025.

He hit the ground running this year, with June's Tour de Wallonie only the second UCI-ranked race of his career after the Antwerp Port Epic in May.

"I was riding there with broken ribs, because I had a bad fall 2 days before the opening stage," he told . In August, there was another top ride in Limousin, where he finished second on the opening day before winning stage 3.

"After my second place in the opening stage, I wanted to win one of the remaining 3 stages at all costs. And in the third stage, I struck gold," he said.

"After the opening stage, I suddenly started receiving messages from teams. But I never thought I'd actually secure a spot – especially after reading an article about how many riders were still without a team for the season."

Soudal-QuickStep were among the teams to show interest, though they were already full for 2027. Choosing Picnic PostNL was a no-brainer, he said, despite recent reports of a 'culture of fear' at the team.

"When the moment finally came to put pen to paper with Picnic PostNL, I didn’t have to think twice. I had a good feeling right from the start of our conversations. They prioritise the riders' interests and are always open to feedback," he said.

"Sure, it’s a strict team, but name me one WorldTour team that isn't. As a team, you have expectations of your riders, and vice versa. That dynamic can – and should – be a bit strict, provided it’s handled fairly."

Depuydt sees himself as a puncheur who excels on shorter climbs while also sprinting well from a small group. He's hoping to race on his home training roads at Amstel Gold Race next season, and is dreaming of racing alongside his idol, Wout van Aert – a goal which shows just how far he's come since his plumbing days.

"I see myself as a puncheur. Short climbs suit me thanks to my past as a mountain biker. But I have also noticed this year that I am fast. I am not a pure sprinter; I am too light for that. But after a tough race, I can finish well in a reduced group," he said.

"I've never ridden a race with Wout. I would think it's really cool if that happens next year. If we stand at the start of a race together, I will look for Wout and ride behind him for a bit to take a look at him.

"If I could just follow him for a little while on a climb, that would be a huge dream come true."

items.title: WorldTour team ignored by new Collective Cycling Group reform project
items.author: Patrick Fletcher
items.content:
The nascent Collective Cycling Group (CCG), a coalition of teams bidding to overhaul cycling’s economic model, did not seek the involvement of all the WorldTour teams, with Human Powered Health telling they were ignored by the project.

The CCG, which is the new version of the failed One Cycling movement, launched publicly on Wednesday, with 24 teams coming together in a bid to "unlock the value potential of professional cycling".

Not all 32 teams from across the men’s and women’s WorldTour agreed to sign up to the new company, with Tadej Pogačar’s UAE Team Emirates the most notable of the teams who have declined to be involved.

However, one WorldTour team, Human Powered Health, were not even approached.

A spokesperson for the US outfit, which has operated in the Women’s WorldTour since 2022, told that senior management were not made aware of the CCG nor of any opportunity to take part in such a project.

The complete overlooking of an established WorldTour team raises early question marks over the unity of the CCG, which was described by its CEO Oliver Ciesla as a “broad and inclusive initiative”.

Furthermore, it was not billed as a closed shop, with the announcement stating that discussions with other teams are ongoing.

The project is largely made up of WorldTour teams but two second-division men’s outfits, Pinarello-Q36.5 and Tudor Pro Cycling are shareholders in the company, too.

Contacted on Friday in relation to Human Powered Health's position, a spokesperson for the Collective Cycling Group said: "CCG has brought together a significant group of leading professional cycling teams, and we are open for that group to grow over time."

With summer behind us, thermal bib tights back in rotation, and a winter of hiding from the rain on Zwift on the horizon, that can only mean one thing: Black Friday is fast approaching.

Like mine, I expect your inbox is full of Black Friday promotions, and the latest to land in mine is a huge Black Friday Wahoo rundown; a list of everything we can expect from Wahoo Fitness, the cycling tech mainstay from Atlanta.

Wahoo's own Black Friday sale kicks off today - November 20th - with deals across smart trainers, indoor bikes and treadmills, but there are plenty of other deals if you know where to look.

So no matter if you're shopping for a new smart trainer, a bike computer, a heart rate monitor, or even a treadmill, you're in the right place to find the best price and the best advice.

If you want to take it a step further, you can add on the Zwift Ride v2 smart frame too. This still uses the Kickr Core v2, but the frame replaces your bike, saving you the need to wheel it through your house. It's also more widely adjustable, so you can share it with others in the house. View Deal

Wahoo is slowly branching out into running, and the Kickr Run is its first foray into treadmills. I've not used it, but the general consensus is that it's very good. View Deal

Whether running or cycling, if you're doing it indoors you'll want a really good fan to help keep you cool. This is still the gold standard in that space, and although the price is steep, mine is still running strong after seven years of regular use. View Deal

This is a bit of an odd one as Amazon says its retail price is 624.99. That's not true, it's actually $499.99. However, it's still a nice discount on the biggest model in Wahoo's GPS computer range. View Deal

In our opinion, it's likely the best for most people. Great navigation, great features, and very user friendly. View Deal

This one's the smallest model in the range. It's perhaps more of a racer's choice, but it also packs more or less all the features of the Roam into a smaller package.

That means it's cheaper still, but the smaller screen can be limiting in some cases. View Deal

This is the same as the product above, but with the Zwift Cog and Click add-on, which replaces the cassette with a single-speed cog that's compatible with all modern groupsets. The 'Click' then lets you shift virtually in-game, which is silent, unlike the loud clunk you sometimes get from a derailleur. View Deal

But before you commit to the V6, consider this, which is potentially better and currently the same price.

The Kickr Move uses the same internals as the current Kickr smart trainer, but adds a moveable track to allow you to roll forward and backward under high load, and a few degrees of left-right tilt too.

In use, the left-right tilt makes for a slightly unusual ride feel, since it doesn't self-centre like a bike. I often felt I was fighting it with core strength or simply sitting at an angle. View Deal

The Zwift Ride V2, paired with Kickr Core 2, is the whole-bike indoor solution, saving your own bike from the wear and tear. Its broad adjustability also means you can share it with others in your home, or try out new positions without changing the fit on your main bike.View Deal

If you want to go even more premium than the Zwift Ride and Kickr Core pairing, this Kickr Bike Pro is it. It's broadly adjustable, tilts back and forth to mimic gradients, it's belt-driven so had a completely silent operation, and shifting is silent too. View Deal

Or a halfway house between the two, the Kickr Bike Shift, which offers the quiet operation and broad adjustability, but foregoes the tilting and a few other features to keep the price down. View Deal

Wahoo is primarily a cycling-focussed company, but it's slowly branching out into running, and this Kickr Run is its first foray into treadmills. View Deal

The Kickr Climb lets you simulate gradients of up to 20%, by literally lifting the front of your bike up and down, to make things feel all the more realistic. It's a useful addition to your setup if you're trying to train for riding up long climbs and you want to mimic the position. View Deal

The Roam barely needs an introduction. It's the goldilocks GPS in Wahoo's range, balancing price, screen size and battery life nicely. View Deal

This one's the baby of the range. More of a racer's choice, but it also packs more or less all the features of the Roam into a smaller, cheaper package.View Deal

And finally, if you want the biggest screen possible for your bike computer then it has to be the Elemnt Ace. It's really very large, the battery is bigger, but of course, so is the price. View Deal

You can easily make do with a simple fan for indoor training, but if you want to have a better time you can get a smart fan like the Kickr Headwind. It'll either work as a dumb fan (just turn it up and down as needed) or you can set it to increase power in line with with your heart rate monitor, so it'll blow stronger the harder you ride. From aero pockets made on a dining table to skinsuits worn by Mark Cavendish – How one rider took Nopinz from Devon to a world-leading 'everyday aero' brand
items.author: Andy McGrath
items.content:
A couple of thousand years before bike racing even existed, Plato had it right: necessity is the mother of all invention.

An elite racer in the UK finishing at the sharp end of the country’s time trials on highways and byways, Blake Pond was getting into an unwanted routine. He would lovingly spend several minutes getting his race number pinned perfectly for every time trial. It was a need, driven by aesthetics, aerodynamics and fastidiousness.

When he jumped on the bike, rode off and heard a ripping noise, he knew what it meant: gigantic pinholes in a speed suit which had cost a week of his bike shop mechanic wages. The alternative fate was just as undesirable: he would pass riders with numbers flapping like parachutes. "On the drive back, I was thinking there’s got to be a better way of doing this," Pond tells over coffee.

His solution: a stretchy pocket, as you’d find on a documents-enclosed envelope, stuck on a skinsuit with special adhesive. Initially, the idea went in his training kit drawer for a few years, doubting its mass appeal. But he was drawn back to it after hearing other racers airing their frustration or even yelps of pain from competitors accidentally getting stuck by a pin-wielding friend trying to give them perfectly flat race numbers.

In 2014, Nopinz was born with the SpeedPocket. At first, it was just Pond, his computer and a heat press. The next iteration involved using a seamstress to sew in this aero addition before posting the garment back.

In little more than a decade, his company has gone from the dining room table in the Devon town of Bideford in the south-west of the United Kingdom and a self-explanatory brand name to more than 50,000 orders and the WorldTour, with a range of apparel and aerodynamic accessories tailored for TT, road racing, triathlon, running and indoor cycling. The WorldTour teams and riders supported along the way include Mark Cavendish on his record-breaking 'Project 35' stage-win quest at the Tour de France.

Nopinz wouldn't be where it is today without the community’s explosion of interest in aero gains over the last decade. "How optimised everyone’s got in TT is crazy. When I was racing back in 2014, I had a lot of watts but not a lot of aero," Pond reflects. "And now it’s shifted the other way completely. I’m going the same sort of speed as I was back then, off 15 per cent less power."

An aero obsessive, Pond climbed a lamppost at the 2015 Tour de France prologue in Utrecht to take photographs of riders from above. This obsession feeds their comprehensiveness, testing products in the wind tunnel at Silverstone, prototyping in-house and doing fabric tests.

WorldTour recognition for 'everyday aero' kit

"We always test and market the averages. If we test at 40, 45 and 50 [km/h] and nought to seven degrees of yaw, we’ll average it out across the speeds we’re aiming that product at," he says, implying that they do not cherry-pick certain data for marketing. Alongside the weighted model designed to better reflect real-world riding conditions that he mentions, theirs is a competitive price point: their popular Sonic socks cost £24.99.

Pond has tried to keep their pricing reasonable, though he is aware of the perverse "reassuringly expensive" philosophy that can pervade in the sport. More expensive does not necessarily mean better. "We need to make the margin in the suit and obviously get profit out of it, but it comes to a stage where you’re making it up, really. Sometimes that does happen with other brands – I can’t understand why the suits are so pricey when we can do it [for cheaper] and do all the R&D," he says.

For the founder, Nopinz suits are for the person who can’t spend £20,000 in a wind tunnel. "Maybe we’re doing it more cost-effectively. There’s a ceiling price: we want to be that reliable sort of partner: you know you’re getting a really good product and it’s not stupidly expensive. That’s how I see it really: NoPinz – everyday aero."

As the framed and signed jerseys around their HQ in the Devon town of Barnstaple attest, the WorldTour wanted a piece of their watt savers too. Starting with support for LottoJumbo-NL in 2015, riders from the likes of FDJ, Israel-Premier Tech and AG2R have all benefited. Alex Dowsett bought his own skinsuits from the company and wore one to win a 2020 Giro d’Italia stage.

The company became an official TT partner to WorldTour team Intermarché the next season, giving it visible "additional credibility" after years of secretly supplying ingredients to the bunch, without recognition or under an NDA.

Pond says Nopinz was offered a full clothing partnership with the Belgian squad but couldn't accommodate the approximate £500,000 outlay, nor the quantity of kit. "That sort of commitment would be crushing," he says.

Still, teams or riders came calling with projects – and you might be surprised at how disorganised and last-minute pro cycling can be. One of the company’s latest nights on the job involved working with takeaway boxes after Israel-Premier Tech realised several days before the Tour de France start that they had sent the wrong designs for their special edition skinsuits. One of their coaching team drove from the south of France to Devon, got a few hours’ kip in Pond’s campervan while Nopinz put on a production run of 50 suits, turning it around in 24 hours in time for him to drive to the Grand Départ.

Cutting-edge materials and UCI pushback

There is a knick-knack sign in Pond’s home which says 'One bike ride away from a good mood'. He was inspired to get in the saddle by hearing tales of the sport: his grandfather, Lew Pond, was a rival of British track sprint icon Reg Harris and was selected for the 1948 Olympics in tandem racing.

After starting in triathlons, he moved to the family’s legacy sport and quickly noticed his bike leg was his strongest. Becoming an elite-licensed racer, he finished seventh in the British national TT championships, although being knocked off by a car led to a back injury which stopped competition between 2014 and 2024. Now back pinning on numbers using his own SpeedPocket – and winning time trials galore in the UK’s south-west – being in the racing environment helps him to understand his customer base and generate ideas.

Pond regards himself as a "fake CEO" and more a hands-on, jack of all trades, doing everything from business direction, budgeting, R&D, product design and social media to fixing machines, using his old bike mechanic nous. Reinvestment in his company has often been preferable to status symbols: when he had the money to consider buying himself a Porsche, a new laser cutter for Nopinz took priority.

Investing in the cutting-edge was worthwhile for their latest skinsuit, the Hypersonic Mk2, building on their original, double-layered (base layer and skinsuit) aero iteration. "We dared to be a bit different with it," he says.

Top speed-suits use a lot of the similar striped fabric on the sleeves, which he dubs 'Super Stripe'. Pond and Nopinz collectively spent four years looking for an aero, textured fabric that would be faster.

A year and a half ago, he found his Eureka material from a company on Italy’s Lake Como and christened it Speedcell. It wasn’t cheap, coming in at roughly £45 a metre at orders of 250 metres minimum, but worth every penny. From a rudimentary aero test, switching from the former material to the new one, the basic prototype showed measurable gains, and they made improvements to the fit. It looks different – sci-fi, even – it feels different, and their testing proved that it saved watts.

An ongoing challenge for Pond is keeping up with UCI regulations. In 2022, the sport’s governing body banned the SpeedPocket at mass events after a consultation with a working group of manufacturers. It was a bitter pill to swallow. "Brands started to cotton on to it and were doing their own versions, but the trouble was, you could hardly see the numbers," he says.

Economic challenges, sustainability, and 'Project 35'

Governing body caprices are just one blast in the face for a business that has faced "one headwind after another" in the last five years.

The vast majority of the cycling industry can relate.

He estimates raw fabric costs have risen "15 to 20" per cent, likely due to the increasing cost of oil and the raw materials used. War has a knock-on effect, with the Russia-Ukraine conflict causing a spike in prices.

Shipping costs have also risen considerably, and Brexit added complications. While Pond produces in the UK, fabrics are bought from European nations or ones outside the continent, bringing pressures associated with import and export.

"Because the industry has been so negative and there’s been so much discounting, you can’t pass it on or win it back," he adds.

From Nopinz’s side, wage inflation and increased National Insurance contributions have added approximately £90,000 to their wage bill across a team of 15, which has been streamlined in recent years.

It all means the customer feels the pinch. A European client will have to pay VAT and additional tariffs as well as possible fuel charges and surcharges from delivery operators, even though Nopinz do customs duties and taxes paid now (i.e. settled by the sender) to try to mitigate nasty surprises. With all the added costs, a would-be buyer might easily abandon their shopping basket and drop off. "That’s been quite hard to navigate," Pond says.

It has become harder to manufacture in the UK and make a profit. Nopinz has been flat in terms of growth in recent years, but making a profit, which he perceives to be rare. "We’d obviously love to see Nopinz go back on that growth trajectory, but we don’t want to do it at the expense of being a sustainable business," he says.

In a crowded market of apparel makers at similar price points, Pond expects they will focus more on the high-end side of the sport and the pinnacle. "I feel that’s where we can differentiate ourselves as a brand," he says.

"We want to have products that people go ‘I’m racing, this is super important, I’ve trained really hard, and I want to make sure I invest in the kit.’ We want them to think Nopinz when it comes to cycling products."

"Being small is good. We’ve got the Speedcell now, and we’re already looking for the next thing – we’ve acknowledged we’ve done that, now someone else is going to do that, and the only way we can stay one step in front is being able to rapidly prototype and produce something," Pond says.

"In a company with a lot more management and structure, it might take two years for a product to be conceived and actually find its way to market. Whereas for us, it can be 10 days if we have to, like something to do with Cavendish."

Ah yes, collaborating with the greatest sprinter in the sport. As office dogs Rodney and Cassandra pad in and out of the HQ boardroom to the whirr of air compressors, Pond locates a pair of surprisingly small white shoes with a blue Nike tick which belonged to the sprinter extraordinaire.

Yes, Nopinz was part of 'Project 35'. Nopinz brand ambassador Alex Dowsett, a fellow aero geek, went to the wind tunnel with Cavendish in the middle of 2024 and called Pond, wanting to fine-tune every possible aero gain in his pursuit of the record.

Turning round prototypes and testing them at Silverstone rapidly, Nopinz worked up toe overshoes ('Hypersonic Tovershoes') and eye-catching textured, shoelace covers. "We tried to simulate the texture of the laces, while also tidying up the aero around the Boa [dial]," he says.

There was also what would become the Hypersonic Mk2 socks, initially called P35, with V-shaped aero chevrons. However, Pond was mindful that, due to UCI equipment rules, anything used for competition has to be on the market. "I said ‘put them on [the website] for £1,000 so nobody buys them’ – and somebody did," he says.

Nopinz also contributed a road race suit for lead-out man Michael Mørkøv and Cavendish. Optimised for hotter conditions using graphene, according to Pond, the Manxman rode it for the sweltering first day across Italy, where he was nearly eliminated in the time cut.

"Unfortunately for us, just not on the stage he won," Pond adds. "But it was super cool to be involved and asked at the eleventh hour, and have someone of Mark’s level and standing. He did ride most of that Tour in our stuff."

Whether it is for road racing’s greatest fast man or the rider looking to win the town sign sprint on the club ride, Pond is constantly thinking about how to get ahead of the competition with his 'everyday aero' apparel. So, what is the future of high-performance clothing in racing?

He imagines fabrics that adjust their own textures to different speeds in the real world. "There are already fabrics that can control how they react electronically, so you can imagine that with a speed suit or something where the texture changes as they go from 30km/h to 50km/h. Optimising itself as you’re riding."

He likens them to people in Tron-style suits, a bit like when Nike did Back to the Future auto-closing shoes. Good luck getting that one past the UCI.

items.title: MLB, college sports, and the sports propaganda moment
items.author: John Griffin
items.content:
When we’re in school, we hear a lot about propaganda. American history textbooks show us political cartoons from the late 19th and early 20th century about the abolition of slavery, the rise of industrial robber-barons, and the progressive movement. European art historians discuss how Louis XIV used paintings and sculptures to present himself as the “Sun King” as he strengthened the power of the French crown over the First and Second Estates. In my own Roman history classes, I spend multiple weeks demonstrating how the emperors employed literature, history, sculpture, and construction projects to assert the supremacy of both Rome and the imperial household. Whether in middle school, high school, or college, students regularly grapple with propaganda in their history classes, learning how people with access to communicative resources have been able to present their own version of reality to sway public opinion in their favor.

Once we’re out of school, though, propaganda falls by the wayside, and ceases to be a concern. It exists, in the public consciousness at least, not as a part of our lives, but as a historical oddity, the behavior of a bygone era — or, when it’s acknowledged in the modern world, as something that happens in the nebulous “over there,” not “here.” And yet, what else can we call the flood of political advertisements in every commercial break that made the World Series borderline unwatchable if not propaganda? After all, are they not trying to sell their version of reality, as opposed to that of their opponents, in an effort to sway voters?

Propaganda is most often understood in terms of politics, but it doesn’t have to be. And right now, we’re living in what I call a sports propaganda moment, as two major entities — the NCAA and Major League Baseball — have gone on the figurative warpath, spending millions of dollars in advertising not to get people to watch their product, but to generate outrage from fans on their own behalf against that of their players.

Whether you’re a fan of a power conference school who competes for the national championship every year or a small liberal arts college who celebrates when their team gets blown out during the March Madness tournament because that meant they made it in the first place, you’ve almost certainly been exposed to commercials sponsored by the Saving College Sports organization in support of the Protect College Sports Act. Since the start of the 2026 college football season (and in truth, since last bowl season, as commercials in support of the bill ran even before it was officially introduced in Congress back in June), they have run a massive ad campaign encouraging fans to contact their congressional representatives and pressure them to vote yes on the bill. Backed by multi-million athletic programs and employing household names such as Deion Sanders and Nick Saban (a current coach and a former one, respectively), these ads center the conversation about the bill on the legitimate concerns fans have about today’s Wild West NIL era — namely, the constant transfers — while ignoring the fact that the bill attempts to, as much as legally possible, reassert the extreme levels of control that the conferences and schools used to have over their athletes.

Starting in the middle of the summer, Major League Baseball has rolled out their own ad campaign in preparation for the upcoming lockout, which is now just a week and a half away. Focused on MLB.tv and social media, the “Level the Playing Field” campaign directly argues for the implementation of a salary cap and floor, claiming that the league cannot have competitive balance due to the payroll disparities that exist between small- and large-market teams. These ads ran all summer, during the All-Star Game festivities, the postseason, the World Series, and the awards season. While, ironically, this meant that the league plastered everywhere a chart in which the team with the second-highest payroll, the Mets, missed the playoffs as the team with the second-lowest payroll, the Rays, won the pennant, the very fact that the league spent time and energy publicly fighting the players during what should be the biggest annual celebrations of the sport is a testament to their priorities — and the important role that these ads played in their pre-lockout preparations.

Now, obviously, these two situations aren’t 100 percent comparable. Decades of corruption and a refusal to negotiate common sense solutions with its players forced college athletes to turn to the courts for assistance, and once the courts got involved, federal involvement and oversight was all but guaranteed, and all the political machinations that entails. Major League Baseball, meanwhile, is attempting, for the second time this decade, to use the expiration of the Collective Bargaining Agreement as an opportunity to break the power of the players’ union and implement the salary cap that they believe will see franchise values skyrocket. Sure, the almighty dollar may be the driving force for both the NCAA and MLB — both the Protect College Sports Act and the salary cap are, at their core, attempts to rein payrolls in and ensure cost certainty — but each organization is so fundamentally different from the other that their financial systems are incomparable.

Nonetheless, the fact that both collegiate athletics and professional baseball have adopted the same tactic, large-scale propaganda campaigns meant to turn the fans against the players, reflects the unique historical moment we are in. As we saw during the last CBA negotiations, social media has allowed players to interact with fans directly, allowing them to, for example, directly argue against the league’s propaganda, much like Jameson Taillon did last week.

Last time around, this direct connection between players and fans appeared to help the players in the negotiations, as the players were able to successfully mock the league’s insistence on removing all evidence of players’ likenesses on all media. That being said, should there be a disconnect between the fans and the players, this has the potential to backfire on the players, and perhaps this is what Major League Baseball is going for here. Baseball may be in the midst of a renaissance, but that doesn’t mean the fans don’t think that some things need to be fixed. Deferred money, especially when done to the extent the Dodgers have in recent years, has been regularly mocked in baseball-related online spaces. The rise of gambling has resulted in real, concrete ethics concerns. Blackouts, TV restrictions, and an ever-increasing stable of required streaming services have made watching the games a veritable chore. Solving none of these problems requires a salary cap, and yet, the league has tried to use their media machine to tie all of them to it, to limited success. In fact, it may have backfired just a bit: the frequency with which they have said “this proposal is contingent on the players accepting a salary cap” has sparked quite a bit of mockery online.

Of course, what has sparked such a large push for a cap at this time is the fact that this CBA negotiation might be the league’s best guaranteed opportunity for one in the foreseeable future. The Dodgers and the Mets have giftwrapped the league two bogeymen to use to sway fans to their side in the negotiations: between the former’s willingness to exploit deferred money and their acquisitions of Shohei Ohtani, Yoshinobu Yamamoto, Rōki Sasaki, Blake Snell, Kyle Tucker, Edwin Díaz, Tanner Scott, Tyler Glasnow, Teoscar Hernández, and Tarik Skubal over the last three years, and the latter’s willingness to ignore all luxury tax thresholds and common sense to sign whatever hot free agents they can, there’s quite a bit of ammunition to turn fans of small- and medium-market teams against the owners. The Players’ Association, meanwhile, has been in a bit of disarray this year, with Tony Clark one of several union executives shown the door within the last 12 months; while it’s unclear whether this will actually harm the union in negotiations, turmoil at the top can at least give the impression of weakness to an ownership group looking to make major gains.

Together, these scenarios have things ripe for Major League Baseball to push all their chips to the center of the table and try to get their salary cap, as it might be their best opportunity for a while. And so, the propaganda machine spins on.

items.title: 'There is certainly no bitterness' – Case against truck driver who struck and killed Davide Rebellin won't continue due to his ill health
items.author: cyclingnews@futurenet.com (Dani Ostanek)
items.content:
The hearings into the case of Wolfgang Rieke, the truck driver who struck and killed Davide Rebellin, have concluded with no charges brought.

Two years ago, a first-instance trial concluded with Rieke being sentenced to a four-year jail term after hitting and killing Rebellin in 2022. However, the Venice Court of Appeals ruled last week that Rieke is unfit to participate in an appeal trial, so the case has been dropped, according to the news agency.

Rieke, 66, currently resides in a nursing home after suffering a stroke in 2024, and this summer his lawyers obtained a doctor's report on his psychological and physical ability to participate in the trial. The report concluded that Rieke is mentally unable to stand trial.

"The family acknowledges what happened. There is certainly respect for the judicial decisions and today's. There is certainly no bitterness; there is acknowledgement and respect for his health," said Rebellin's family's lawyer, Davide Picco.

"Justice has certainly worked, given that the Prosecutor's Office transferred the defendant from Germany to Italy. He served several months in prison and then under house arrest. His health condition then led to today's sentence."

Rieke, who had previously pled guilty to a non-fatal hit-and-run and drunk driving, struck and killed Rebellin as he was on a training ride in Montebello Vincentino on November 30, 2022, shortly after he retired from racing. He then fled the scene, leading authorities to launch a multi-country search.

He turned himself in to German police in June 2023 and was later handed a four-year sentence after the judge rejected several initial plea deals. After suffering a stroke two years ago, the case against him will not continue.

"We are satisfied that the judges have accepted our requests, acknowledging Mr. Rieke's current health conditions, which prevent him from consciously participating in the trial," said Rieke's lawyer, Andrea Nardin, according to the Corriere del Veneto.

The road season might be at an end, but Cyclingnews isn't slowing down. Subscribe for unlimited access to our comprehensive news coverage, industry-leading CN Labs testing, expert columnists, and so much more. Plus, the Cyclingnews app means you can stay up-to-date wherever you go!

items.title: Knicks 102, Timberwolves 99: “3 straight on the road, what’s up…”
items.author: Moritz Wollert
items.content:
LaMelo Ball hit one of his patented three-pointers from the left elbow early in the third quarter against the New York Knicks last night and as the crowd cheered, he proceeded to jog back on defense. Of course, the only not totally broken Ball brother couldn’t let the moment pass without completely indulging himself into a thoroughly scripted “ice in the veins”-gesture that feels as original these days as a two-handed set shot. Just a moment later Josh Hart rained on the parade, running directly by Vanilla Ball’s D and finishing an easy backdoor cut with a simple layup. And just like that the Knicks were up 14 again, ignoring the protocol of how cutting a deficit to 12 in a game where your team got handsomely dominated up to that point needs to be celebrated.

It feels good to root for a professional team, doesn’t it? It will allow you to say things like Real Clydes Wear Plaid shared in the and which I unapologetically stole for the headline of this recap. The Knicks won their third game in a row at Minnesota last night and they probably made it a lot harder than it needed to be. Their opponents certainly had something to do with it, no matter how ill-advised some individual emotions might have been. The Timberwolves can play tremendous defense, are as long as those trees in their logo and have an aggression you could certainly link to that name-giving animal of them. They got a good albeit cranky coach, a proven system, years of winning experience. Yet in the end they also got LaMelo Ball now.

Knicks hold off Minnesota’s late rally

We get that he is a talented, at times iconic passer; we also get that he has found his footing fairly well on the frozen tundra near the Great Lakes so far. But we really can’t get convinced that you can ever really win big with a “talent” like that. His play can remind one of the game young kids play before they really get a hang of Dr. Naismith’s rules. They also take two steps before every dribble, then four after they pick the ball up. They also couldn’t care less about a repetitive shooting motion or dribbling the ball without palming it every time. With the kids it’s okay and fun, we let them discover themselves as players and excuse it. But Lamborghini LaMelo should be held to a different standard, he is supposed to be a professional NBA player after all.

Luckily for the Knicks, they got plenty of real pros on their roster, guys who truly care about winning and treat their profession like it means something – not only to them but to others. It certainly seemed that way when they played most of the game last night with a level of calmness and concentration that has been a hallmark of theirs ever since they went on that beautiful championship run last year. But despite all their dominance over that two-month stretch in the playoffs, you can’t ignore that they are a team with plenty of cracks in their armor, many of which showed themselves last night as well. It’s the kind of weakness that are often the reason for the Bockers falling behind big only to have the opportunity to stage their beloved monumental comebacks later on.

Knicks’ defense wins it in the end

Yesterday the Knicks offense completely bogged down late when Minnesota went to more switching on D (raise your hand if you’ve seen that before), neutralizing all the beautiful team basketball that helped the Gotham Gang run up an almost 20-point lead earlier. Not even Karl-Anthony Towns, once again mesmerizing for most of the night against a traditional five at his old stomping grounds, couldn’t regain his first-half form. Maybe he rode the pine a little long, Mr. Brown? Well, you can’t play him all 48, we get it. A lineup that included Jose Alvarado, Andre Drummond and Josh Hart was still an interesting choice, to say the least. For all the individual chops it’s quite a load for Jalen Brunson to carry that group offensively, it almost feels like him heaving big AD up K2 or some other majestic mountain. It might get you to the summit against certain defenses but considering some defenses are as long and physical as the Wolf Pack, it can also get cold rather quickly. Especially when Brunson still hasn’t found his touch inside the paint yet.

That New York could still pull it out in the end is a testament to timely plays and a gritty, opportunistic defense that at no point in the game relented to the physically imposing Wolves coming at them. When LaMelo Ball couldn’t find someone open downtown, the canines’ only plan was to ram their oversized combo forwards ahead. It worked here or there but never consistently. Watch out, there’s an extended arm coming at you – boom, another offensive foul! It’s an interesting yet understandable choice by the league to make the off arm a point of emphasis this year (sorry, SGA). Why didn’t they do the same for palming the basketball or taking more steps than a dressage horse? Your guess is as good as mine.

For the moment, though, let us not worry about it – there is a win to be celebrated. For all we know though, our guys are probably watching some film right now and preparing for their next opponent (Portland on Saturday). Maybe they are also speeding race cars through some busy pedestrian zone or practice their one-legged step-back fadeaway jumper that has netted them less than 42 percent shooting for their career?

Nah, we leave that to the guy with ice in his veins.

items.title: Today on Pinstripe Alley – 11/20/26
items.author: Madison Pavich
items.content:
We’re less than a week away from Thanksgiving now, and the Yankees have started to get a bit active before the holidays kick in. After locking down David Bednar’s contract for 2027, there were overnight musings that Jonathan Loáisiga reportedly is coming back to New York after a year away in Arizona. His 2026 season was excellent, and it was also the first healthy season he’d had in a while, but up until now it seemed like there was more interest from the Dodgers or Mets than the Yankees. If they managed to get a hometown discount for their former reliever then they might’ve gotten away with a bit of a steal, but we’ll have to wait and see what the actual details of this potential deal are.

We’ve got a few things in store for you today, beginning with John giving us his thoughts on MLB’s early PR propaganda laying the ground for their side of the upcoming lockout. Jonathan hands out our latest report card to the rookie George Lombard Jr. after his whirlwind second half with the big league team, Kevin remembers the legacy of one of baseball’s early titans in Clark Griffith, and then in the afternoon I’ll be back to answer your latest mailbag questions.

1. If the Yankees have Jonathan Loáisiga back in the fold, how many games do you expect to see him in next year?

2. Do they still need another established reliever in your mind, or do you trust Brian Cashman and Matt Blake to make due from here?

items.title: Why a 37-year-old Primož Roglič is still a great signing and how more freedom at NSN can unlock his five-time Grand Tour-winning best
items.author: James Moultrie
items.content:
The further into the off-season it went, the more likely it seemed that five-time Grand Tour winner Primož Roglič's career was going to end before he wanted it to.

It wasn't like most of the big-name moves in modern cycling, which are signposted months in advance, but it did finally bring an answer to the question that Roglič had been answering with "We'll see, ah" and "I don't know yet" ever since July, when Red Bull team boss Ralph Denk confirmed he would be leaving.

The idiosyncrasies that have made him one of the peloton's most popular and compelling riders won't be going anywhere, instead just repackaged in the Swiss team's colours for, as they described it, the "final chapter".

Though it should be noted that Roglič hasn't ruled out a similarly complicated re-up of his time in the sport 12 months from now, more openly putting it down to needing "some time to figure out how to make a chapter in my life where I am peaceful, but the answer is actually simple with the team name: Never Say Never."

Tudor, Pinarello Q36.5, Unibet Rose Rockets, and XDS Astana were among the other speculated landing spots for the Slovenian, but clearly none could muster up the perfect mix of financial resources, a fitting contract, or the desire to bring him in, but NSN have found room for the GC star.

Importantly, it means that instead of a nondescript 68th-place finish at Il Lombardia, 37-year-old Roglič is now in control of where his final chapter as a professional comes to an end, and he certainly won't be looking to go out with a whimper.

"I still believe I have some work to do – in both racing and with myself," he said, when his surprise move to NSN was announced on Wednesday evening. "I have the drive and also the attitude not just to race, but also achieve things."

After his home heroics in Slovenia late in the season, Roglič will start his 12th year in the WorldTour as the reigning European time trial champion, which he wasn't even sure he'd get to wear in a race after he won it: "Maybe I'll only wear it at home. Because we haven't decided yet what I'll do next, but no matter what, I'll wear it."

Off the bike for 10 days and unsure if he would have even taken the start if it wasn't where he lived, Roglič's late-season results should be looked at with the context that what he did was nothing short of miraculous when it came to recovery. This is far from the sort of moves that saw the then Israel-Premier Tech – which was rebranded as NSN a year ago – criticised as something of a "retirement home".

Roglič may be a veteran, but he is still one of the top riders in the world.

Roglič raced 53 times in 2026, with mixed success, but importantly, still with success.

He opened up his campaign with a solid performance at Tirreno-Adriatico, finishing fifth overall and helping teammate Giulio Pellizzari to third on GC behind winner Isaac del Toro, and followed that up with more success in Italy by taking third at Milano-Torino.

From here, things slowed down for the Slovenian, finishing 16th at Iztulia Basque Country, and failing to impress at the Tours de Romandie and Suisse as compatriot Tadej Pogačar dominated the racing to take both titles. Roglič only managed 18th and eighth overall, respectively.

He turned things around at the Slovenian national championships, ramping up his performance with a win in the ITT and fourth in the road race, ahead of his already confirmed major goal of the Vuelta, where he was looking to stand alone at the top of the history books for the most overall titles – which he currently shares alongside Roberto Heras on four.

However, it was soon after, on July 31, that Roglič revealed he had been halted in his plans: "Got hit by a car few days ago…" read a post on his Instagram. "I won't be participating in San Sebastian and in Burgos unfortunately... not the best scenario, but it's life, eh. Now it's all systems go towards La Vuelta; we work and hope things will turn around!"

He did make it to the Vuelta, and while there were no of old – as it was Enric Mas who stepped into the spotlight and claimed red after Pogačar crashed out – when all was said and done in Granada, Roglič could only describe second as feeling "like a victory to me".

Mas rightly took the majority of headlines as he made history for Spain, but there was a more visceral reaction from the press room as second-place Roglič answered his final question in the longer post-race press conferences. It felt like a goodbye to the race where he had enjoyed his most successful moments, with no one in the room, nor he, knowing where he'd end up next as the room filled with applause and matching gratitude from the Slovenian.

The same feelings returned at European Championships and Il Lombardia, where the enigmatic Roglič was none the wiser, still saying, "You never know when is the last one. Like everything in life, it can be a bit emotional," as he conceded that the Italian Monument could be the endpoint.

Into the off-season, Roglič next resurfaced at the Taiwan Cycling Masters, where a KOM challenge south of Taipei saw the Slovenian drop no hints at whether he'd signed a contract – instead, he continued to be cryptic in his comments.

"The people that you collect on the way, or they collect you, that you have around, they help the influence at the end on you," he said in a promotional video for the event.

"I think yes, they left a mark on me, like I said I'm always open to learn, to know more, and the more you know, the more you know that you don't know, so it's a never-ending process."

Well now we do know, as does he, that life in the pro peloton will be continuing, and while those previously ruthless punchy legs perhaps lack the same bite they had five-eight years ago, he has a diesel engine that can still power him up the highest mountains.

In his best results at the Europeans and Vuelta, it's key not to forget that it wasn't against weak fields by any means; at the former, Bruno Armirail, Stefan Küng, and Jakob Söderqvist were among those unable to live with Roglič's time, and at the latter he emerged ahead of Giro runner-up Felix Gall, new teammate Richard Carapaz, and Oscar Onley for his second place on GC.

How he could fit into NSN's plans

Even with Roglič clearly proving his worth as an asset into his late 30s, there still remains the question of how NSN will deploy their new leader and fit him into their schedules after such a late pick-up.

The team's media day is next week, and the thoughts will already be on December and January training camp ahead of the start of the 2027 season on January 1, with rider schedules among the news set to be confirmed in the coming weeks.

With Carapaz, Santiago Buitrago, and Lennert Van Eetvelt, NSN had already been looking to improve their stock as a GC-hunting outfit, having failed to finish in the top 10 of all three Grand Tours in 2026. Their best results were 12th at the Giro, 68th at the Tour, and 15th at the Vuelta, but with those three mentioned above and Roglič, they suddenly have a chance at finishing in the top 10 and potentially higher of all three.

Carapaz has already suggested that it is a return to the Giro where he wants to target an overall placing, and while this would seem to interfere with a potential Slovenian homecoming for Roglič, it's actually the Tour and Vuelta that look like more likely targets.

Sharing the leadership among their new star signings lessens any chance for internal bickering, and also opens the door to Carapaz potentially chasing GC at one Grand Tour and then stages and the mountains classification at another – as he'd been doing successfully for EF in recent years.

NSN's new foray into the GC hierarchy also represents more freedom for a rider like Roglič, who has been bitten by bad luck and crashes several times in the most pressure-filled moments riding for Visma and Red Bull – teams where you to maintain GC success to keep your spot.

Roglič should get the freedom to pick the plan which suits him best and allows him to build up in the ways he knows will work for GT success. NSN will also offer up what Red Bull didn't in his final Vuelta for them this past summer, where a young team lacking in climbing support saw them struggle to front up numbers to muster a major challenge consistently against Mas – even if it likely would have had no effect on the final red jersey standings.

NSN can commit their younger riders Buitrago and Van Eetvelt, and the experience of George Bennett and Nick Schultz to a full-blown Roglič bid, be that at the Tour or Vuelta. And while in an age of Pogačar, Vingegaard, Evenepoel, Seixas, and Del Toro, any entrance into the top-five seems unlikely, this summer proved that anything can happen, even to the big stars, with Pogačar crashing out of the Vuelta and Vingegaard from the Tour, so it's not out of the realms of possibility that he is able to score one final Grand Tour podium, which would be his 10th, or indeed a sixth victory.

In reality, Roglič's goals could become a final stage win at the Tour – to add to the three he already has, 10 years after his first into Serre-Chevalier on stage 17 of the 2017 race – the GC title at the Tour de Suisse, which remains the only major one-week stage race missing from his palmarès from the seven, or indeed that elusive fifth Vuelta title.

Even with Pogačar probably taking the start, living by the words "Never say never" has got Roglič this far, and he'll be hoping his new team's name can carry him to the last hurrah which he deserves. There's a degree of risk in not allowing that European title win on home roads to become the denouement to his great career, but as one Slovenian famously said en route to one of his Vuelta titles: "No risk, no glory."

Castro, just 23, became a minor-league free agent after playing in the Red Sox system since 2019, was a little underwhelming with an 88 wRC+ in 119 games for Triple-A Pawtucket, but per FanGraphs boasts above average power both raw and in-game. Knicks 102, Timberwolves 99: Scenes from a beautiful game with a funky tail
items.author: Russell Richardson
items.content:
The Timberwolves (11-5) have been the talk of the West, especially with their level of success given the absence of star guard Anthony Edwards (knee). Coach Chris Finch has his crew chucking up 116.7 points per game while also leading the league in rebounding and fielding the top defense. So far this season, the Wolves have held every opponent to under 50% from the floor—and they would again tonight. New York (9-6) knew the trouble that awaited them as they squared off with their first Western Conference team of the season. The game started with runs in either direction, but the Knicks gained steam and took a 15-point lead into halftime. In the third quarter, Minnesota chipped away at the lead, and Jaden McDaniels led the doggies on a rally in the fourth quarter to cut the lead to three with a scant few minutes left. But neither team could buy a bucket down the stretch. The Knicks went scoreless for the final three and a half minutes, the T’Wolves missed on everything, and the visitors escaped with a 102-99 victory.

That’s the lowest score for the Wolves this season. Take a bow, fellas.

On a first-quarter drive, LaMelo Ball (your favorite Ball brother?) swiped an arm across Jalen Brunson’s face. Cap was rattled by it and subbed out around the nine-minute mark, giving Tyler Kolek an unusually early appearance. With Jalen out, the visitors went on a 12-0 run. The backup guard was terrific in his first-half play, dishing five dimes in seven minutes, a third of the team’s total, and leading a second unit that tallied 17 first-half points.

A game of runs! Minny responded with a 13-2 run that included Ball attacking the paint for points and Jaden McDaniels swishing from long range. McDaniels was Minnesota’s most efficient scorer in the half, putting up 11 points on perfect 4-of-4 shooting, including three triples (but also three costly turnovers). Returning the favor, Josh Hart dropped a triple that started an 11-3 run and gave New York a 33-26 lead at the break.

In the second quarter, KAT and OG Anunoby stepped further into the spotlight. They combined for 30 first-half points on 12-of-18 shooting. Karl sang beautifully on his former home court, scoring 17 points and hauling in eight boards in just 16 minutes; OG chimed in with 13 points and a pair of blocks. Jose Alvarado got a little run but was quiet in the quarter. In a nice return to form, Josh Hart added nine points on 3-of-4 shooting from deep, while steady-eddie Landry Shamet provided a major lift off the bench with 10 points and a team-best plus-17 in 17 minutes.

The T’Wolves have length that can really clog the lane, and that explains why Jalen Brunson managed just seven points on 2-of-8 shooting, with his two makes coming from the outfield. Against most teams, Cap performs his string music in the paint, but these Minnesota trees make for a dense forest. Also underwhelming: Mikal Bridges, who threw the ball at the basket just once in his 11 minutes before intermission. It’s sort of wild that the Knicks posted 65 first-half points despite getting only nine points from their starting backcourt.

Also weird: Rudy Gobert had just five points and one rebound in his first 15 minutes. In fact, the Wolves’ starting frontcourt of McDaniels, Jonathan Kuminga, and Gobert combined for two rebounds. Believe it, Ripley! They weren’t the only stinkers on the home team. Ball, Kuminga, and Ayo Dosunmu combined to shoot 4-of-17 through the half. Minnesota shot a respectable 44% overall and 39% from three, but outside of McDaniels, nobody found much rhythm. With the Knicks shooting a blistering 57% from the field and an eye-popping 63% from deep (10-of-16), the good guys were ahead 65-50 at intermission.

In the third quarter, Brunson shouldered the load, scoring 14 points in the period, and Bridges showed up to sink a three and commit two thefts. Towns continued to crash the glass but cooled off somewhat offensively, as did OG. For the home team, Kuminga poured in 14 points, making two three-pointers while blocking three shots. The Wolves couldn’t put together a sustained run, though. Trailing 83-66 with around 3:30 left, they outscored our heroes 12-7, cutting the score to 90-78 at the break.

To start the final frame, Kolek converted a four-point play to give the guests a 16-point lead. But we never thought the Furballs would roll over and die—and no, they didn’t. As New York’s offense stalled (e.g., Towns missed four of five, which he redeemed with three stuffs), McDaniels, Trey Lyles, and the Wolves chipped away at the lead. After New York went ahead 97-85 with 7:56 remaining, Minnesota scored eight unanswered points, including a McDaniels three and a Ball pull-up triple, to cut the lead to four. The Knicks went nearly four minutes without scoring, prompting a timeout and the return of Bridges and Anunoby.

What makes tonight’s win most stunning is that New York managed to achieve it despite going scoreless over the final 3:26. During that grisly stretch, KAT copped a flopping tech, Gobert slammed an alley-oop, and Ayo buried a three, bringing the Timberwolves within three with 2:34 left. Brunson missed a pull-up jumper, New York committed a shot-clock violation, Towns was called for an offensive foul with 1:04 left, and Bridges missed a turnaround jumper with 23 seconds remaining.

The hosts had plenty of chances to tie or steal the lead but couldn’t capitalize. Ball bricked two shots in the final 1:39; Dosunmu whiffed a bunny; and Bridges blocked Gobert’s putback attempt with 44 seconds left—arguably the biggest defensive play of the game. Ball blanked on a potential tying longball with 10 seconds remaining, and Kuminga collected the rebound but threw the ball away, with Landry Shamet securing the steal to end Minnesota’s night.

For those keeping track at home, the Timberwolves missed their final six field-goal attempts and committed five turnovers over the last five minutes. That’s a lot of ugly basketball to taint what was otherwise a quite pleasant viewing experience. But a win’s a win! And this one came over a very worthy opponent.

The Knicks host the Blazers on Saturday. Mo is sewing arms and legs onto your recap. Safe travels, Knickerbockers.

After three Premier League defeats on the spin, Manchester City need something or someone to come along and put some pep in their step, and Fulham look like just the thing – after all, in the past 15 years these teams have played 20 times in all competitions, and City have won precisely 20 of those games. Their current run of 17 successive league wins against Fulham is the longest run of victories by one club against a single opponent in English top-flight history. It is a reflection of the changing realities of English football, and the gulf that has opened between the teams that dominate it and those who seek to challenge them, that of the top 10 such runs all but one occurred in whole or in part after 2010 and six of them have been achieved by Sheikh Mansour’s Manchester City, with Chelsea responsible for another two, Manchester United one, and Portsmouth’s postwar, 13-game supremacy over Everton – a wild ride that included two 5-0s, a 5-1, a 6-3 and a 7-0 – the anomaly.
